path_blood.prompt: Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood. Why are they called arteries?
options: rich
Arteries must always carry oxygen-rich blood.
Oxygen content varies with the circuit. It does not define an artery.
away
They carry blood away from the heart.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart.
lungs
Every vessel connected to a lung is an artery.
Pulmonary veins also connect to the lungs. Direction relative to the heart distinguishes arteries from veins.

path_blood.prompt: After gas exchange in the lungs, where does blood go next?
options: right
To the right atrium through the venae cavae.
The venae cavae return blood from the body. Blood from the lungs enters the left atrium.
ventricle
To the right ventricle through pulmonary arteries.
That reverses pulmonary arterial flow. Pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
left
To the left atrium through pulmonary veins.
Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

path_air.prompt: What crosses between alveolar air and nearby blood during gas exchange?
options: gases
Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across a thin barrier.
The gases diffuse across the air–blood barrier. Blood remains in capillaries.
bubbles
Whole air bubbles enter the blood.
Normal gas exchange transfers gas molecules, not air bubbles, into blood.
diaphragm
Air passes through the diaphragm into the blood.
The diaphragm helps change chest volume. Gas exchange occurs at the alveoli and surrounding capillaries.

path_air.prompt: During quiet breathing at rest, what helps air flow out?
options: contract
The diaphragm contracts and flattens.
This enlarges the chest during inhalation. Quiet exhalation follows relaxation of inspiratory muscles.
relax
Inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs recoil.
Elastic recoil reduces lung volume, raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure so air flows out.
gravity
Gravity pulls all air downward out of the lungs.
Airflow follows a pressure difference. It is not defined by an upward or downward direction.

path_food.prompt: Which route carries feces out of the digestive tract?
options: rectum
Rectum → anal canal → anus.
Feces pass through the rectum and anal canal to the anus. Urine leaves by a separate route.
bladder
Bladder → urethra.
The bladder stores urine. The bladder and urethra are urinary structures, not the route for feces.
gallbladder
Gallbladder → small intestine.
The gallbladder stores bile used in digestion. It does not store or expel feces.

path_food.prompt: How do intestinal villi support nutrient absorption?
options: chunks
They let large food chunks pass directly into blood.
Nutrients must cross the intestinal lining. Whole food chunks do not normally enter blood.
block
They block all movement through the intestine.
Villi line the intestinal wall; they do not seal the passage through the intestine.
area
They increase the surface available for absorption.
Villi and microvilli provide more absorptive surface within the intestinal lining.

path_nerve.prompt: In this example, which nerve carries sensory input from the palm side of the index finger?
options: sciatic
Sciatic nerve.
The sciatic nerve serves the lower limb. It does not carry sensation from this finger.
median
Median nerve.
The median nerve carries sensory fibers from this part of the index finger toward the spinal cord.
femoral
Femoral nerve.
The femoral nerve serves parts of the lower limb, not the hand.

path_nerve.prompt: How can withdrawal begin without waiting for a conscious decision?
options: circuit
Spinal circuits link sensory input to motor output.
Spinal circuits can initiate the reflex while information also travels toward the brain.
muscle
The muscle makes a decision without nerve signals.
Muscle fibers respond to motor signals. They do not replace the sensory and spinal parts of this reflex.
never
No information about the stimulus ever reaches the brain.
Information also travels upward for perception, and brain pathways can modify spinal reflexes.
